newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan surplus rises in February helped by weak yen.
newsitem.headline: Japan surplus rises in February helped by weak yen.

text.p: The surplus in Japan's current account, the broadest measure of trade in goods and services, rose 15.4 percent to 865.2 billion yen ($6.92 billion) in February from a year earlier, the Ministry of Finance (MOF) announced on Monday.

The figure was slightly higher than economists' average forecast of a surplus of 801.1 billion yen ($6.40 billion), but was largely in line with their expectations of a rise brought on by the weakness of the yen.
The surplus in merchandise trade alone rose 2.9 percent to 878.0 billion yen ($7.02 billion) from the same month a year earlier.

"(It shows) good evidence that Japanese exports benefit from the gain in competitiveness, as well as a pick-up in global demand. Head winds (for the Japanese economy) from external account contraction have turned into tail winds and should start to contribute very well to economic growth," said Jesper Koll, chief economist at J.P. Morgan.
But the surplus figures were mostly shrugged off on trading floors, and 20 minutes after they were issued the dollar rose to a 50-month high, boosted by buying from Japanese investors and traders.
The greenback climbed as high as 124.83 yen, its highest since February 1993.

The spotlight has swung back on to Japan's current account data after a rise in the nation's customs-cleared trade surplus in February for the first time in over two years, followed by comments by U.S. officials voicing concern over a return to the days of a ballooning Japanese surplus.

Last Friday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin urged Japan to guard against a resurgence of its trade surplus, though he rejected suggestions that a stronger Japanese currency was the best way to do that.
"We don't believe in anybody using their currency for trade policies -- us or anybody else," he said.
But Rubin added that there was great interest around the world in what additional strategies Japan might take if it failed to avoid a resurgence in its current account surplus.
Although a MOF official admitted that the pace of the decline in the current account surplus was slowing, he said he thought the trade surplus was still declining overall.
But J.P. Morgan's Koll said: "I expect the current account surplus, which now stands at about 1.5 percent of GDP (gross domestic product) to, by the end of this year, stand at about two percent."

The Finance Ministry also said on Monday that Japan's customs-cleared trade surplus in the first 20 days of March fell 33.8 percent from a year earlier to 337.48 billion yen ($2.69 billion) compared with a revised surplus of 509.51 billion yen ($4.07 billion) in the same period last year. ($1=125 yen)
